bib.title: Ensemble Learning (Chapter 16, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed.)

question: How can a collection of simple base models be combined, and why do boosting and lasso-style L1 regularization explain ensemble success?
hypothesis: Boosting with shrinkage behaves like an L1-regularized (lasso-like) path over a huge tree dictionary, so ensembles can be learned in two stages: generate diverse trees, then lasso-post-process them.
contributions: Error-correcting output codes as an ensemble
Forward stagewise regression as lasso analogue of shrunken boosting
ISLE and rule ensembles (Friedman and Popescu)

results.claim: Lasso post-processing of a 1000-tree random forest on spam data keeps about 40 trees and matches gradient boosting.
results.source: Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman ESL 2nd ed. ch. 16 (own simulation)
results.setup: Spam data; random forest of 1000 trees grown to max depth, m=7; lasso applied to the first 500 trees; test error vs number of nonzero-coefficient trees
results.quote: reduces the forest to about 40 trees, rather than the original 1000
results.note: Fig 16.6 caption says post-processing used the first 500 trees; text says forest of 1000. No numeric test errors printed (read from figure only).

results.claim: Modified random forest (5% subsample without replacement, ~six terminal nodes) cuts training cost about 100-fold but post-processed performance falls short of the full random forest.
results.source: Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman ESL 2nd ed. ch. 16 (own simulation)
results.setup: Spam data; each tree grown on 5% random subsample without replacement, shallow (~6 terminal nodes), then lasso post-processed

results.claim: ISLE on spam data (eta=1/2, nu=0.05, 5-terminal-node trees) does not improve test error but cuts the number of trees by a factor of five.

results.claim: AdaBoost test error on mixture data is minimised at 240 trees and overfits dramatically if run to convergence (10,000 trees, margin settled).

results.claim: Random ECOC code assignment works as well as optimally built codes; the benefit is variance reduction.
Boosted classifiers form an L1-regularized monotone path to a margin-maximizing solution, which can be a poor overfit end point; early stopping should use a validation set.
results.setup: Summary of Schapire 1998, Raetsch and Warmuth 2002, Rosset 2004a, Hastie 2007

results.claim: Bet on sparsity principle: use a procedure that does well in sparse problems, since no procedure does well in dense problems.
results.setup: High-dimensional problems; qualified by target, dictionary size, training size, NSR

limits: Simulations only (spam, mixture, prostate, synthetic); Fig 16.2 picks lambda by test error (oracle), not CV
Most comparisons are read off figures; few numbers printed
Fig 16.8 vs Rulefit comparison is not like-for-like (CV used for Rulefit)
Lasso and FS0 paths equal only if coefficients monotone / basis uncorrelated
Chapter does not cover modern gradient boosting libraries (XGBoost, LightGBM)
practices: Treat bagging, random forests, boosting, stacking and dictionary methods as ensembles of base learners (p.605).
Use shrinkage (small nu) in gradient boosting rather than nu=1; subset-selection-like no shrinkage is too greedy (p.610).
Bet on sparsity: prefer L1-type procedures in high dimensions (p.611).
Stop boosting early using a validation set, since the margin-maximizing end of the path can overfit (p.616).
Post-process a tree ensemble with the lasso to shrink the model, choosing lambda by cross-validation (p.617, 620).
Subsample without replacement with eta<=1/2 (and ~1/sqrt(N) for large N) and nu=0.1 to get diverse trees (p.619-620).
Add rules from trees and original variables to the dictionary before lasso (p.622).

Error-correcting output codes: one classifier per column of a coding matrix; delta_k(x)=sum_l |C_kl - p_l(x)|

infinitesimal forward stagewise, limit eps->0; fits a monotone lasso

set of indicator rules derived from every node of every tree, then lasso-fit
